title: August 20 — Listening Section 3
transcript:
PART 3 - Varroa Mite and Types of Bees

NARRATOR: Section 3. You will hear two researchers comparing their research on different types of bees. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer Questions 21 to 25.

SPEAKER 1: I had a chance to look at your research yesterday. Is any of this relevant to my research?

SPEAKER 2: Yes, at least one aspect. My main research interest is the European honey bee and the problems facing it.

SPEAKER 1: Yes, I've heard about the Varroa mite, but I don't know much about it.

SPEAKER 2: Well, the mite wiped out a large proportion of the European honey bee population in North America back in the 1990s. Fortunately, it hasn't caused the same problem here.

SPEAKER 1: It sounds like such a little creature.

SPEAKER 2: It certainly is. It's like a little hitchhiker. When a bee lands on a [[Q21|flower]], the mite can get off and wait there until another bee comes along. It then climbs onto that bee.

SPEAKER 1: Right.

SPEAKER 2: The mite then hitches a ride back to the [[Q22|hive]] with its new host.

SPEAKER 1: So the mite actually sneaks inside the hive on top of the bee?

SPEAKER 2: That's right. Once inside the hive, it dives into a honeycomb cell and hides at the bottom. That's where the queen bee lays an egg.

SPEAKER 1: I'm interested to know why the bees don't detect the mite.

SPEAKER 2: That's the interesting part. It uses the [[Q23|honey]] to cover its own smell, so it isn't detected. Then it feeds on the [[Q24|blood]] of the bee larva.

SPEAKER 1: So this happens while the baby bee is developing?

SPEAKER 2: Exactly. The mite's reproductive cycle takes place inside the cell. When that's finished, it leaves.

SPEAKER 1: It sounds like a clever enemy. But why does it have such a devastating effect on bee populations?

SPEAKER 2: Well, it leaves the bee debilitated and also infected with a [[Q25|virus]] that can spread amongst the colony, so the population can die out.

SPEAKER 1: That could have a devastating effect on agriculture.

SPEAKER 2: Yes. The worrying thing is that we need to find ways of increasing bee populations.

NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.

SPEAKER 1: Well, as we can combine my research on native bees with yours, perhaps we should try putting together a research proposal and find a way of increasing bee populations.

SPEAKER 2: That would be great. Let's start with the European bumblebee. There was talk recently about bringing them into this country.

SPEAKER 1: Yes, but the problem is that the European bumblebee has a tendency to [[Q26|spread weeds to new areas]]. We don't want to introduce another environmental problem.

SPEAKER 2: True. What about the Blue Banded Bee? It could be useful to farmers.

SPEAKER 1: That's one of the challenges we face, because [[Q27|not much is known about it yet]]. There hasn't been a lot of research on the species.

SPEAKER 2: Then bringing in Africanised bees would be disastrous.

SPEAKER 1: Definitely. The Africanised bee was introduced to South America because it was a good honey producer, but what people didn't realise was how [[Q28|aggressive]] it could be - it may attack almost anything that moves.

SPEAKER 2: Speaking of honey producers, the Australian Stingless Bee is quite good.

SPEAKER 1: Yes, although it doesn't produce as much honey as some other species. The main drawback with stingless bees is that they're [[Q29|very sensitive to temperature]]. They won't survive if it gets too cold, so they need a warm climate and aren't really suited to the colder southern parts of Australia.

SPEAKER 2: And what about the Canadian Leafcutter Bee?

SPEAKER 1: I think that one has a lot of potential for farmers. It's a gentle, hard-working bee. They've been imported to pollinate lucerne or alfalfa crops. At the moment, production here is much lower than in North America, where they use these leafcutter bees.

SPEAKER 2: So why don't we import more of them?

SPEAKER 1: Research shows that the bees have to be imported in [[Q30|very limited numbers]] and carefully checked for pests and diseases before they're released. The drawback is that the numbers are still too few to make much difference to farmers' crop yields. It takes time to build up the population.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
